Small states face a distinct set of constraints when they plan the transition to clean electricity. Goa, for example, buys most of its power from central stations and from other states, and its coastline, forests, and farmland leave little room for large ground-mounted plants. This study compares centralised and decentralised supply options for the state over a twenty-year horizon. We model hourly demand, rooftop generation, wind variability, and the price of battery storage, and we test each option against three criteria: cost, reliability, and land use. The results suggest that rooftop solar paired with short-duration storage could meet about a third of demand by 2040 at a lower levelised cost than new thermal contracts. Neither option, however, removes the need for imports during the monsoon, when solar output falls sharply. These findings point to a mixed strategy in which the state builds local capacity while it renegotiates long-term purchase agreements. The same approach may help other land-constrained regions that rely on imported electricity.
